title: AI-Generated 'Odysseus: The Fall' Challenges Nolan's $250 Million Epic at a Fraction of the Cost
excerpt: A 135-minute film made with Chinese AI video software for roughly $50,000 attempts to ride the buzz around Christopher Nolan's box-office smash 'The Odyssey.'
body:
Key Takeaways
  • AI-generated film 'Odysseus: The Fall' costs about $50,000, a fraction of Nolan's $250 million budget.
  • The film, created by Ash Koosha, will be available for rent at $9.99 this summer.
  • Nolan's 'The Odyssey' opened to $257.8 million globally with a 95% Rotten Tomatoes score.
  • Critics highlight significant visual flaws in the AI film, calling it a tech demo rather than a serious contender.

Article data
  • A 135-minute AI-generated film called 'Odysseus: The Fall' will release this summer, made for roughly $50,000 using Chinese AI video software Kling.
  • The project is by Ash Koosha and production company Fountain 0, whose previous AI film 'Dreams of Violets' premiered at the 2025 Tribeca Film Festival.
  • Christopher Nolan's $250 million live-action 'The Odyssey' opened to $257.8 million globally with a 95% Rotten Tomatoes score.
  • Critics have dismissed the AI version as a tech demo lacking object permanence, with characters changing appearance between shots.

While Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is shattering box office records with a $257.8 million global opening weekend, a far cheaper challenger is preparing to ride its wake — a fully AI-generated feature film that cost a fraction of one percent of Nolan's $250 million budget.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=55IrrpiXGqQ

Odysseus: The Fall, a 135-minute film created by Iranian-born musician and AI filmmaker Ash Koosha through his production company Fountain 0, was built using Kling, a Chinese AI video-generating tool, and the company's own proprietary software. Its budget sits in the "mid-five figures" — approximately $50,000 — and it will be available to rent for $9.99 on Fountain 0's website later this summer.

A Modern Mockbuster — or Something More?

The film follows Odysseus on his journey home from Troy but takes a darker, more abstract approach than Homer's original. Its creators describe it as "the fractured memory of a drowning man in his final minutes — a voyage that is really a trial, where every monster wears his own handwriting." The synopsis promises an ending "where the songs never go: not with a hero's welcome, but with forgiveness offered by the one person who knows exactly what he is."

Koosha is not new to AI filmmaking. His previous work, Dreams of Violets, a 74-minute film about suffering under Iran's regime, premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival in 2025. That project worked around AI's fundamental limitation — the inability to maintain object permanence across scenes — by employing a vignette structure that drifted between characters and moments rather than tracking a single consistent narrative.

"We very much hope that Christopher Nolan's film, The Odyssey, is a raging success at the box office, and in some way that our version of the journey of Odysseus might further that success."

— Ash Koosha, creator of Odysseus: The Fall

The Technical Limitations

Critical Reception of AI Film
›'Odysseus: The Fall' criticized for visual inconsistencies.
›Characters change appearance between shots.
›Described as a tech demo rather than a full narrative.
›Visuals acknowledged as impressive for AI-generated content.

Early reactions to the trailer have been mixed at best. While the visuals are acknowledged as impressive for AI-generated content, critics point to fundamental problems: Odysseus does not look the same from shot to shot, characters change shape and color between cuts, and interactions between two figures on screen remain unconvincing. Kotaku described it as "incredibly impressive-looking for something made by AI" before cataloguing its many visual failures.

The timing of the release is clearly no accident. Nolan's The Odyssey, starring Matt Damon as Odysseus alongside Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Zendaya, and Robert Pattinson, opened on July 17 to both critical acclaim (95% on Rotten Tomatoes, A CinemaScore) and massive commercial success. Nolan himself has been vocal about his opposition to AI in filmmaking, recently using the term "slop" to describe generative AI content.

The Bigger Debate

The project has reignited the ongoing argument about AI's role in creative industries. As tech commentator Dylan Beattie framed it at a recent conference: "If you had a machine that could build houses in six hours instead of six weeks, would you be going around trying to get people to invest in your machine, or would you just be building houses and selling them?"

The implication is that Odysseus: The Fall functions less as a standalone work of art and more as a tech demo — a proof of concept designed to sell Fountain 0's AI tools to other creators. Whether the 135-minute runtime can sustain viewer interest beyond the initial spectacle of its AI-generated imagery remains to be seen.

For the film industry, the broader question is not whether this particular AI film can compete with Nolan — it clearly cannot — but what happens when the technology improves enough to solve the object permanence problem and generate consistent characters across a feature-length runtime. That day is not here yet, but each new project narrows the gap.
